{{short description|American mathematician (1855 to 1934)}}
{{Redirect-distinguish|Arthur Hathaway|Arthur Hathaway Hewitt}} 
'''Arthur Stafford Hathaway''' (1855 — 1934) was an American [[mathematician]].

Arthur was born September 15, 1855, in [[Keeler, Michigan]].<ref>J. McKeen Cattell & Dean A. Brimhall (1921) [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/title/3786#page/316/mode/1up American Men of Science], page 298, link from [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]</ref>

A student at [[Cornell University]], Hathaway earned a [[bachelor's degree]] in 1879. For two years he was instructor in mathematics at Friends High School in [[Baltimore]]. 
Hathaway studied with [[James Joseph Sylvester]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]]. From Sylvester's lectures he learned some [[number theory]] and published notes on congruences.

He was an instructor at Cornell University from 1885 to 1890 and an [[assistant professor]] in 1891.

In October 1884 [[William Thomson, Baron Kelvin]] led a [[master class]] on "Molecular Dynamics and the Wave Theory of Light" at Johns Hopkins. Kelvin did not provide a text for his course and Hathaway made notes in short-hand. He wrote up the notes and duplicated them with a [[Mimeograph#Papyrograph|Papyrograph]], a recent [[stencil]]-based device. As the demand outstripped the supply, Hathaway corresponded with Kelvin back in Glasgow to prepare for proper publication. After nineteen years the lectures were published.<ref>[[William Thomson, Lord Kelvin]] (1904) [https://archive.org/details/baltimorelecture00kelviala Molecular dynamics and the wave theory of light], twenty lectures transcribed by A.S. Hathaway, [[Cambridge University Press]], link from [[Internet Archive]]</ref> In 1987 Hathaway's original transcription from 1884 was published when Johns Hopkins Center for the History and Philosophy of Science decided to commemorate the centennial of Kelvin's lectures.<ref>Robert Kargon and Peter Achinstein (1987) ''Kelvin’s Baltimore Lectures and Modern Theoretical Physics: historical and philosophical perspectives'', [[MIT Press]] {{ISBN|0-262-11117-9}}</ref>

In [[Terre Haute, Indiana]] Hathaway taught at [[Rose Polytechnic Institute]] until 1920 and published ''A Primer on Quaternions'' in 1896. He became the U.S. national secretary for the international [[Quaternion Association]] in 1899.

==Works==
* 1883: [https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2369228 Some Papers in the Theory of Numbers], [[American Journal of Mathematics]] 6: 316–30.
* 1887: [https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2369331 A Memoir in the Theory of Numbers], ''American Journal of Mathematics'' 9(2): 162–79.
* 1896: [http://www.gutenberg.org/dirs/etext06/pqtrn10p.pdf A Primer on Quaternions] from [[Project Gutenberg]]
* 1897: [https://archive.org/details/jstor-1623392 Review: ''Non-Euclidean Geometry, or the Science of Absolute Space''], by Bolyai, translated by Halsted, in [[Science (journal)|Science]], February 19, link from [[Jstor]] Early Content.
* 1901: [https://archive.org/details/aprimercalculus00hathgoog A Primer on Calculus], [[Macmillan Publishers]], link from [[Archive.org]].
* 1901: [https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1901-07-06/S0002-9904-1901-00797-5/S0002-9904-1901-00797-5.pdf "Pure mathematics for engineering students"], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 7(6):266–71.
* 1902: [https://www.jstor.org/stable/1986315 Quaternion Space], [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] 3(1):46–59.
* 1906: [http://quod.lib.umich.edu/u/umhistmath/ABR5018.0001.001 Analytic Dynamics] from [[University of Michigan]] Historical Math Collection.
* 1920: [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2973244 Dog swims after duck problem], [[American Mathematical Monthly]]  27(1):31.
